You use the subjunctive without a “main verb”: in wishes (Che Dio vi benedica! Magari!), in orders and permissions (Che entri!), in doubtful questions (Che sia già partito?) and in fixed expressions (sia come sia, che io sappia).
if only! / that would be great!
be that as it may; whatever happens
the needle / to thread the needle
If only I were young like you!
Let them come in, the door is open.
Could the train have arrived already?
As far as I know, the frame was never found.
To express wishes with “che” + present subjunctive: Che Dio vi benedica! Che tu possa…
To express wishes that are hard to fulfil with “magari” + imperfect or pluperfect subjunctive.
To give orders and permissions in the third person: Che entri! Che aspettino!
To ask doubtful questions with the subjunctive: Che sia già partito? Che abbia ragione lui?
To use the fixed expressions: sia come sia, che io sappia, costi quel che costi, viva gli sposi, così sia.
To make exclamations with “se” + imperfect subjunctive: Se tu sapessi!
Sorrento, September. Great-grandmother Assunta has just blessed everyone at the table. Pietro writes her sentences down in his notebook and asks her why she speaks “differently”.
God bless you all, and may the pasta not overcook.
Nonna Assunta, may I ask you a question? You use the subjunctive on its own, without any verb in front of it.
And what should I put in front? The verb is there, but it isn’t said. “I hope God will bless you.” I hope it, but I don’t say it.
And when you said “if only I were young like you”?
That’s a wish that doesn’t come true. Magari! It means: I’d like it so much, but it won’t happen.
And “let them come in”, when the neighbours knocked?
That’s a polite order. I’m not talking to them, I’m talking about them. “Let them come in.”
I’m writing it all down. In Florence nobody talks like that any more.
Maybe they’re wrong in Florence. As far as I know, the subjunctive has never died. It sleeps a little, like me after lunch.
Then may it sleep well. And may it wake up early.
In main clauses, the subjunctive appears with no verb in front when we express a wish. The verb “I hope / I wish” is understood.
Che la terra ti sia lieve.
May the earth rest lightly on you.
God grant that he comes back soon!
Viva gli sposi! / Vivano gli sposi!
“Viva” is actually the subjunctive of “vivere”. Grammatically, the plural would be “vivano gli sposi”, but in speech you often hear “viva gli sposi”.
2. Impossible wishes: magari, almeno, volesse il cielo
a wish about the present, unlikely
“Magari!” on its own, as an answer, means “that would be great!”: — Vinci tu? — Magari! Careful: “magari” + indicative means “maybe”: Magari vengo domani = Maybe I’ll come tomorrow.
3. Orders and permissions in the third person
Come in, madam. / Please, have a seat.
The polite imperative (Lei) is actually a present subjunctive: Venga! Senta! Mi dica! Si accomodi! It’s the same mechanism: “I’m talking about you”, in the third person.
A question that begins with “che” + subjunctive expresses a suspicion or a worry: the equivalent of English “could it be that…?”.
Che fosse proprio quella la cornice?
Could that really have been the frame?
Se tu sapessi! / Se l’aveste vista!
If only you knew! / If only you had seen her!
Exclamations with “se” + imperfect subjunctive are really conditionals without the second half: “Se tu sapessi (quanto ti voglio bene)!”
If only I had known earlier!
If only you knew how much I love you!
If only I could come tomorrow!
How do you say “Could she be right?”
Che cosa augura Assunta, oltre alla benedizione?
Che la pasta non si scuocia
Che Assunta usa il congiuntivo da solo
Secondo Assunta, dov’è il verbo che manca?
Un desiderio che non si avvera
Che cosa fa il congiuntivo, secondo Assunta?

Every year, on the twentieth of September, Matei and Giulia went back to Sorrento, to the church of Sant’Antonino where they had married, and every year they went in a different way: once by car with Totò on the back seat, once from Sicily, once from Malta, with a ferry and two planes. That year they went by train, and not alone. With them were Viola, who was six and had a new dress with yellow flowers, Pietro, who had asked for two days off school promising to catch up on everything, and Graziella, who hadn’t left Tuscany for more than five years and whom Dr Neri had allowed to go on one condition written on a sheet of paper: “No cooking. Not even if they beg you on their knees.” Graziella had folded the sheet and put it in her bag, next to the little pot of nepitella she never left at home. On the train to Naples she said only, watching the fields go by: “May this be the time I really rest.” Nobody believed it, not even she.

In Naples they took the Circumvesuviana, the battered little red train that runs along the gulf, between the sea on one side and Vesuvius on the other. Viola was glued to the window counting the boats. Pietro was taking notes in the black notebook. Graziella, on the other hand, looked at the stations one by one, Ercolano, Torre del Greco, Pompei, Castellammare, and at every name she moved her lips, as if reciting a prayer. At one point Giulia asked her whether she felt all right. Graziella smiled. She explained that her mother Lucia had been born round there, in Vico Equense, and that as a child she had made that journey only once, in 1960, for an aunt’s funeral. She remembered the red train, the sea, and a huge lemon a lady had given her at the station. “I never went back,” she said. “If only I had gone back sooner. But the trattoria never closed.” Matei took her hand. “Now it’s closed,” he said. “And you’re here.”

At the Sorrento station Gennaro, Giulia’s brother, was waiting for them with the lemon grove’s old three-wheeled truck, the one they used to carry the crates of lemons. There wasn’t room for everyone. Gennaro put Graziella in the front, next to him, like a guest of honour, and loaded Viola into the back, sitting on a pile of jute sacks among four crates of freshly picked lemons. Viola shrieked with happiness. Giulia protested that it wasn’t safe. Gennaro answered that he and Giulia, as children, had ridden up that road in the back a thousand times and that, as far as he knew, they were both still alive. Matei and Pietro took a taxi with the suitcases. The truck set off coughing up the hill, between stone walls and pergolas, with Viola greeting all the passers-by with a lemon in her hand like a queen with her sceptre. Graziella held on to the handle with both hands and laughed like a girl. “Let nobody tell Dr Neri,” she said. Gennaro promised her absolute silence.

Nonna Assunta’s house was on the hill above Sorrento, at the end of a little stone lane, in the middle of a lemon grove her family had farmed for four generations. It was a low white house, with green shutters and a vine pergola in front of the door, and inside it smelled of lemon, wax and tomato sauce. Waiting to welcome them were Rosaria, Giulia’s mother, who hugged them one by one as if she hadn’t seen them for ten years, Gennaro with his wife and their two children, and a crowd of neighbours and relatives Viola couldn’t count. Nonna Assunta was waiting for them sitting under the pergola, on a wicker chair, with a black shawl on her shoulders despite the heat and her sewing basket on her knees. She was tiny, much smaller than Pietro remembered, and she was almost a hundred years old. But her eyes were the same: black, lively, curious as a little girl’s. When she saw Viola, she opened her arms and said, in her thin, firm voice: “Here she is. God bless her. She’s the image of her great-grandmother.”

Then she saw Graziella, and something happened that nobody expected. The two women had met only once, seven years earlier, at the wedding, and had barely spoken, because that day there were two hundred guests and Bellini had dragged Graziella off to dance. Now they looked at each other for a long time, in silence, like two old generals sizing each other up before a negotiation. Then Assunta pointed to the chair next to hers and said: “Let her sit here, signora. Next to me.” Graziella sat down. Assunta took her hand, turned it over, looked at the palm, the scars from burns, the calluses from the ladle. Then she showed her own: the middle finger bent by eighty years of thimble, the fingertips pricked by the needle. “You fed people,” she said. “I clothed them. May the Lord forgive us everything else.” Graziella laughed, for the first time since she had left Florence. From that moment the two great-grandmothers, as Pietro called them in his notebook, were inseparable. They spent three days sitting under the pergola, talking nonstop, laughing, arguing about the ragù recipe.

It was during the first lunch, under the pergola, with thirty people round a table made of three tables placed in a row, that Pietro began to notice the way Nonna Assunta spoke. Before eating, she raised her hand and said: “God bless you all, and may the pasta not overcook.” When more neighbours knocked, she said: “Let them come in, there’s room.” When Gennaro told her his son wanted to go and study in Milan, she sighed: “If only I were young like him.” And when Rosaria asked her whether it was true that the old parish priest had died, she replied: “As far as I know, last time he was breathing.” Pietro took out the black notebook under the table and began to write. They were all sentences with the subjunctive, but with nothing in front: no “I hope that”, no “I want”, no “I think that”. The subjunctive stood alone, like an old person who no longer needs to lean on anyone. At school they had taught him that the subjunctive was always a dependent clause. Nonna Assunta, evidently, had never been informed.

After lunch, while the adults slept in the shade and Viola chased the hens through the lemon grove, Pietro sat down next to Assunta and asked permission to ask her a question. Assunta, who was sewing a hem, answered without looking up: “Let him ask it, young man. Questions cost nothing.” Pietro explained what he had noticed. Assunta laughed, a dry, birdlike laugh. She told him the verb in front was there, but wasn’t said, because there was no need to say it. “Che Dio vi benedica” meant “I hope God will bless you”: but whoever blesses others always hopes, there’s no need to say it. “Magari” was a wish that doesn’t come true, and you said it under your breath, like a secret. “Che entrino” was a polite order: you aren’t talking to them, you’re talking about them, and so the order becomes an invitation. “When I was young,” she said, “everyone talked like that. The subjunctive was like bread: it was on every table.” Pietro told her that in Florence nobody talked like that any more. Assunta looked up from her sewing. “As far as I know,” she said, “the subjunctive has never died. It sleeps a little, like me after lunch.”

That evening Pietro phoned Bianca and told her everything: the subjunctive that stood alone, the verb that was there but wasn’t said, the subjunctive that slept after lunch. Bianca laughed on the phone. Then she pointed out something he had never thought about. He too used the subjunctive on its own, every day, dozens of times, without realising. In the trattoria, when he welcomed a customer, he said: “Prego, si accomodi.” When he took an order: “Mi dica.” When a customer asked for the bill: “Un attimo, aspetti.” They were all present subjunctives. The polite imperative, the one with Lei, was nothing but a subjunctive in disguise, because when you speak to someone with Lei, in the end, you are speaking about them, in the third person, as Assunta said. Pietro was silent. He was sixteen, he had spoken Italian all his life, and he had never noticed. “So the subjunctive doesn’t sleep,” he said. “It works in the trattoria.” Bianca laughed again. “It works everywhere,” she said. “Only nobody thanks it.”

It was that evening, after dinner, that Assunta told the story of the fragment. Only a few were left under the pergola: the two great-grandmothers, Giulia, Matei and Pietro, with the cicadas singing in the lemon grove and the lights of the coast coming on down below, towards Naples. Giulia asked her to tell again the story of 1943, the one she always told when Giulia was little, the story of the paintings saved from the bombs. Assunta thought for a long time. Then she said that tonight she would tell it differently, because there was a part she had never told anyone. Not even Rosaria. Not even her husband, God rest him. She pulled her shawl tight round her shoulders, opened the sewing basket and took out, from under the reels of thread and the pincushions, a little tin box, the kind for throat lozenges, rusty at the corners. She placed it on the table, in front of Giulia. “First the story,” she said. “Then the box. Let nobody open it before I’ve finished.”

In the summer of 1943, she said, her family lived in Naples, in the Vergini quarter, because her father worked at the port. She was a skinny girl with plaits who helped her mother sew for the ladies of the neighbourhood. Naples was bombed almost every night. People slept in the shelters, in the tufa caves under the city, and every morning they went out to see what was still standing. Near their home there was a little church, Santa Maria del Pozzo, small and poor, with only one painting worth anything: a Madonna painted on wood, with a gilded frame, which the neighbourhood called “the Madonna of the seamstresses”, because the seamstresses brought her flowers every Saturday. The parish priest, don Ciro, had decided to take it to safety in the sacristy, in the crypt. But on the night of the fourth of August, while they were moving it, the sirens sounded. Don Ciro, Assunta and her mother carried the panel down the stairs at a run, in the dark, while the first bombs fell on the port and the ground shook.

On the stairs, in the dark, the frame struck the corner of a wall. Assunta heard a sharp noise, like a branch snapping, and something fell on her foot. She picked it up without thinking and put it in her apron pocket. Then they went on down. They spent the night in the crypt, with the Madonna leaning against the wall and don Ciro praying aloud. The next morning, when they came out, half the neighbourhood was destroyed. The little church was still standing, but the roof had collapsed. Two weeks later Assunta’s family left Naples: they were evacuees, like thousands of other families, and they went back to Sorrento, to her grandfather’s lemon grove. Assunta never saw the little church again, nor don Ciro, nor the Madonna of the seamstresses. Only many years later, rummaging in the apron her mother had kept, did she find the thing she had picked up on the stairs. It was a piece of the frame: a little flower of gilded wood, the size of a fingernail. “I’ve kept it for eighty-six years,” she said. “Every time I looked at it I thought: could the Madonna still be alive? Could they have saved her? And I never had the courage to ask.”

Giulia opened the box. Inside, on a tuft of yellowed cotton wool, was the flower: five petals of carved wood, covered with worn gold leaf, with a fragment of white gesso on the back, where it had come away from the frame. Giulia picked it up with two fingers, the way she had learned to pick up old things, and turned it towards the lamp. She looked at it for a long time, in silence, with the magnifying glass she always kept in her bag. Then she looked up at her grandmother. She said it was a seventeenth-century piece, Neapolitan, carved by hand, with water gilding on red bole, as they did then in the workshops of Naples. She said the fragment of gesso on the back was still intact, and that if the frame still existed, she could recognise exactly the spot it had broken off from, like a piece of a jigsaw. Assunta listened with her hands clasped in her lap. “Well?” she asked at last, in a voice that didn’t sound like hers. “Could she still be alive?” Giulia took her hands. “I don’t know, Nonna,” she said. “But from tomorrow we’ll look for her. Whatever it takes.”

The search began the next morning, at seven, at the kitchen table in Rosaria’s house, with Pietro’s computer, Giulia’s phone and three coffees. Giulia first called the Soprintendenza in Naples, where a restorer she had met years before at a conference worked. The restorer said the church of Santa Maria del Pozzo had been closed in 1950 and then deconsecrated, and that today it was a storeroom. The paintings and furnishings, as far as she knew, had been taken elsewhere, but she didn’t know where. She promised to search the archives. Meanwhile Pietro searched online, in the digital inventories of Neapolitan churches, typing every possible combination: “Madonna delle sarte”, “Santa Maria del Pozzo”, “Vergini”, “tavola Seicento”. Matei phoned Bellini, who knew half of Italy, and Bellini promised to call an old friend at the Diocesan Museum of Naples. Graziella and Assunta, under the pergola, waited. Every now and then Assunta asked: “Could they have found something?” And Graziella answered, with the patience of someone who had waited nineteen days for the Crusca: “Not yet. Old things need time. Like ragù.”

While they waited, the two great-grandmothers decided to settle the question of the ragù once and for all. Dr Neri had forbidden Graziella to cook, but he hadn’t forbidden her to argue about cooking, and Graziella, as Pietro pointed out, had always been very good at finding loopholes in rules. Assunta maintained that Neapolitan ragù must cook for at least six hours, “pippiando”, that is, simmering very gently, with the bubbles appearing on the surface like gossiping neighbours at the window. Graziella maintained that in Florence ragù was a different thing, and that six hours was an exaggeration for people with nothing to do. Assunta replied that whoever doesn’t have six hours for ragù doesn’t have six hours for anything. Graziella replied that in six hours she served a hundred and twenty covers. The argument lasted all morning and drew in Rosaria, Gennaro’s wife and two neighbours, and in the end it was settled with a compromise: Rosaria would cook Assunta’s ragù, and Graziella would add, at the end, a single leaf from a plant she kept in her bag. “Let it be a secret,” said Graziella. Assunta nodded gravely. “So be it,” she replied.

That afternoon, while the ragù simmered on the stove, Viola discovered Assunta’s sewing basket. Her great-grandmother found her sitting on the ground under the pergola, with the reels of thread lined up like toy soldiers, trying to thread a needle. She couldn’t: the thread was too soft, the eye too small, and the fingers of a six-year-old too impatient. Assunta didn’t scold her. She sat down beside her, with difficulty, and showed her the trick: wet the tip of the thread with your lips, cut it diagonally with the scissors, hold the needle against the light and slip the thread through in a single movement, without thinking. Viola tried ten times. On the eleventh the thread went through. Viola shouted with joy. Assunta smiled, then slipped off her middle finger the old silver thimble, worn and dented, that she had worn since she was fifteen, and put it on Viola’s thumb, because it was too big for her middle finger. “May it bring you luck,” she said. “And may you be able to mend everything that tears. Not just clothes.”

The phone call came at six in the evening, while they were laying the table. It was Bellini’s friend, Dr Esposito of the Diocesan Museum, no relation to Giulia, he made clear at once with a laugh, because in Naples there are more Espositos than pigeons. He said he had found, in the inventory of the museum’s storerooms, a record card from 1951: “Madonna and Child, panel, Neapolitan school, 17th c., from the church of S. Maria del Pozzo ai Vergini (deconsecrated). Original gilded frame, damaged: loss in the lower right corner.” The panel had been restored in the eighties and since then had been displayed in a small room of the museum, among other works saved from the city’s closed churches. The frame was still the original one. And in the lower right corner, Dr Esposito added, there was still a gap, about the size of a fingernail, which no restorer had wanted to fill, because nobody knew what the missing piece looked like. Giulia put the phone on speaker. Under the pergola there was absolute silence. Then Assunta said, in a thread of a voice: “Praised be God.”

That night Assunta didn’t sleep. Graziella noticed around one, when she came down to the kitchen for a glass of water and found her sitting under the pergola, in the dark, with the little tin box in her lap. She sat down next to her without saying anything. They stayed like that for a long time, listening to the cicadas and the distant sea. Then Assunta spoke. She said she was afraid. Not of dying: at almost a hundred, she said, death is a neighbour you greet every morning. She was afraid it wasn’t her. That Dr Esposito was mistaken. That the flower wouldn’t fit, and that eighty-six years of waiting would end in nothing. “And what if it’s another Madonna?” she asked. “What if I waited my whole life for nothing?” Graziella took her hand. She told her that she too, for fifty-four years, had kept a little pot on the windowsill without knowing whether one day someone would understand its value. “The things you look after,” she said, “you don’t look after them to know how it ends. You look after them because someone has to.” Assunta squeezed her hand. Then, around three, she fell asleep on Graziella’s shoulder.

On the twentieth of September, the morning of the anniversary, instead of going to Sant’Antonino they went to Naples. All together: Assunta in the front row on the Circumvesuviana, with her black shawl and the little tin box clutched in her hands, and beside her Graziella, who didn’t leave her for a moment. The Diocesan Museum was in a large Gothic church in the historic centre, Donnaregina, with fourteenth-century frescoes on the walls and a cool silence that smelled of stone. Dr Esposito was waiting for them at the entrance, together with a young restorer in white gloves. He led them into a small side room. And there, hanging on the wall, lit by a discreet light, was the Madonna of the seamstresses. She was smaller than Assunta remembered, and more beautiful. The Madonna wore a red dress and a blue mantle, held in her arms a chubby child playing with a reel of thread, and looked down, towards whoever was looking at her, with a tired half-smile. Assunta stopped in the doorway and didn’t move again. Her hands were trembling. “It’s her,” was all she said. “It’s really her. The child with the reel. I had forgotten.”

The child with the reel, Dr Esposito explained, was the reason the neighbourhood seamstresses had adopted that Madonna as their protector. Nobody knew who had painted it: perhaps a workshop painter, perhaps an anonymous devotee, perhaps a tailor’s wife. Then the restorer approached the frame with a magnifying glass and pointed to the lower right corner. The gap was there: a small hollow in the wood, with the white gesso showing, surrounded by other identical gilded flowers, four on each side, all the same except the missing one. Giulia opened the little box, took the flower with two fingers and handed it to the restorer. The young woman looked at it, turned it over, and without touching the frame brought it close to the hollow, holding it a millimetre away, against the light. You could see it perfectly. The edge of the gesso on the back of the flower followed the edge of the hollow exactly, every notch, every crack, like two halves of a torn leaf. The restorer looked up at Giulia, then at Dr Esposito, and said only, her voice full of emotion: “It fits. It fits perfectly.”

For a few seconds nobody in the room moved. Then Assunta took a step forward, then another, leaning on Graziella’s arm, until she stood in front of the Madonna, so close she could have touched her. She didn’t touch her. She crossed herself, slowly, and began to speak to her under her breath, in broad Neapolitan, the way you talk to an old acquaintance you meet in the street after many years. Nobody understood the words except Rosaria, who covered her mouth with her hand. Later Rosaria told Giulia what she had said. She had said: “Forgive me for being late. I’ve brought you something of yours.” Viola, meanwhile, had gone up to the wall and was looking at the child with the reel. Then she looked at her thumb, with the silver thimble. Then she looked at the child again. “He sews too,” she said, convinced. Dr Esposito smiled and said that perhaps she was right, and perhaps that was exactly why the seamstresses had chosen him. The restorer, her eyes glistening, put the flower back in the little box and closed it gently, the way you close a cradle.

Dr Esposito asked Assunta whether she wished to donate the fragment to the museum, so that it could be put back in the frame during the next maintenance work. Assunta didn’t answer at once. She looked at the flower in the restorer’s hand, then at the Madonna, then at Viola, who was standing next to her with the silver thimble on her thumb. Pietro understood that she was reckoning with eighty-six years of waiting, of unanswered questions, of evenings spent looking at that little flower in the lozenge tin. Then Assunta spoke. She said the flower wasn’t hers, and never had been: she had only looked after it, the way you look after something that belongs to someone else until the owner comes back. “Let it go home,” she said. “It’s been away long enough.” But she set one condition. She wanted to be present when they put it back in its place. Dr Esposito looked at the restorer, who made a quick calculation. The work was planned for the spring. “In May,” she said. “If all goes well.” Assunta nodded. “Then may it go well,” she said. “I’ll be there in May. God willing.”

They returned to Sorrento in the late afternoon, and at six, as every year, they all went into the church of Sant’Antonino together. There was no ceremony: Matei and Giulia simply sat in the pew where they had sat on their wedding day, stayed silent for a few minutes, and then lit a candle. That year they lit three. One for themselves. One for Viola. And one, Giulia said, for a girl with plaits who in 1943 had carried a Madonna down the stairs in the dark. Assunta, sitting in the front pew between Graziella and Rosaria, pretended not to have heard, but wiped her eyes with a corner of her shawl. Then, as they were leaving, she stopped at the church door, turned to Matei and Giulia and blessed them, with her hand raised and trembling, as the parish priest of her childhood used to do. “May you grow old together like the trees of the lemon grove,” she said, “which bear more fruit the older they get. May you never lack bread, nor work, nor patience. And may your daughter be more stubborn than both of you.” Matei laughed. “On that point,” he said, “the blessing has already worked.”

That evening Assunta’s ragù, with Graziella’s secret leaf, was served under the pergola to thirty-two people, and everyone said it was the best they had ever eaten. Assunta and Graziella looked at each other with the satisfied air of two generals who have won the same battle from two different sides. At the end of dinner Gennaro raised his glass and shouted: “Viva gli sposi!” Assunta corrected him at once: “Vivano. There are two of them.” Everyone laughed, and from that moment, for the rest of the evening, every time someone made a toast they shouted “Vivano!” in the plural, with exaggerated emphasis, looking at Assunta, who pretended to be offended and was in fact very happy. Later, when Viola fell asleep in Matei’s arms with the thimble still on her thumb, Pietro sat on the steps of the house, under the stars, and opened the black notebook. At the top of a new page he wrote: “The subjunctive that stands alone.” And underneath, one by one, all of Assunta’s sentences from those three days. There were twenty-seven. He counted them twice.

On the day of departure Assunta walked with them to the gate of the lemon grove, leaning on Rosaria’s arm, and said goodbye to each of them. To Matei she said: “May the Lord keep your hands safe.” To Giulia: “May you always find what you are looking for.” To Pietro, who had read her the list of twenty-seven sentences, she said, laughing: “May you teach them to all of Florence, young man, so the subjunctive wakes up.” To Viola she said nothing: she hugged her tight and closed her hand over the thimble. Then it was Graziella’s turn. The two great-grandmothers stood face to face for a moment without speaking. Then they embraced, for a long time, like two old friends who have known each other forever and not for three days. “Let’s see each other again in May,” said Graziella. “In Naples. For the flower.” Assunta nodded. “Magari,” she said. Then she corrected herself at once, with a flash in her black eyes. “No. No magari. We’ll see each other in May. Come what may.”

On the train home, between Naples and Rome, Graziella slept almost the whole time, her head against the window and her bag held tight on her knees. Giulia watched the sea receding. Viola played with the thimble, putting it on and taking it off every finger, one after the other. Matei read. Pietro, instead, reread the notebook. When he reached the last page, he added a line beneath Assunta’s twenty-seven sentences. He thought about it for a long time before writing it, because he wanted it to be right. Then he wrote: “Twenty-eight. Said by me, on the train, watching my grandmother sleep: may she live to see that flower go back to its place.” He reread the sentence. It was a subjunctive standing alone, with nothing in front. No “I hope that”, no “I wish that”. But the verb in front was there, as Assunta said. There was just no need to say it. He closed the notebook, leaned his head against the seat and looked out of the window. Vesuvius had disappeared behind the hills. But Pietro knew it was still there, even if you couldn’t see it. Like the verb. Like Nonna Assunta, far away, under the pergola. Like the flower, waiting for May.

Madonna and Child. Painting on wood, Neapolitan school, seventeenth century.
From the church of Santa Maria del Pozzo ai Vergini, closed in 1950 and deconsecrated.
Original gilded frame, damaged during the bombings of 1943: loss in the lower right corner.
Note: the Child holds a reel of thread. Popularly known as “the Madonna of the seamstresses”.
